The honour roll included Agatha Christie and her archeologist husband, Sir Mortimer Wheeler, and Professor Giuseppe Tucci, together with ambassadors, writers and travelersâthe house was rarely without visitors. After retirement, he headed the project for the preservation of Mohenjodaro and served as the first chairman of the Authority for the Preservation of Mohenjodaro, one of the worldâs earliest settlements.

The present figure depicts the bodhisattva Manjushri seated in padmasana with his hands raised in the dharmachakra ('turning of the Wheel of Dharma') mudra. Unlike more common depictions of the deity with sword upraised, the present figure represents the deity's 'undefiled' manifestation with the Wisdom Sword and Prajna-paramita Sutra floating above his shoulders.

The present dish belongs to a very rare group of vessels produced at the Ding kilns with finely fluted interior sides and flattened lobed rims with a raised edge. Due to their fragility and their being fired upside-down (fashao), very few successfully fired examples of this type survive and are almost all still preserved within the imperial collections. Compare a dish of identical form and design preserved in the Palace Museum, Beijing, in Selection of Ding Ware. The Palace Museumâs Collection and Archaeological Excavation, Beijing, 2012, pl. 120; another slightly larger impressed with a tortoise, crane and flying immortal, pl. 121; and another dish of more generic floral design excavated from a Ding kiln site in Xiheliu, Quyang county, in Ding ci yishu [The art of Ding porcelain], Shijiazhuang, 2002, pl. 150.
Among the most important English writers of the early twentieth century, Somerset Maugham (1874â1965) possessed a particular interest in Chinese works of art. Following a four-month journey to China from 1919 to 1920, Maugham is said to have brought a suitcase of artifacts back to London which, in the following decades, came to fill his residence Villa La Mauresque in the south of France from 1927 until his passing in 1965; see Ray Zhou, âGlobal Modernism Reconsidered: W. Somerset Maughamâs Journey to the Eastâ, PhD Thesis, University of Sydney, 2025, pp 169â170. A portrait of Maugham, at ease in his study at La Mauresque in 1939, depicts the present dish in full view on the authorâs desk, evidence of his close personal affection for the piece.

description_block:
These delicately painted panels represent the new styles pursued by porcelain artists upon the fall of the Qing dynasty. With imperial orders discontinued, craftsmen in the porcelain center of Jingdezhen were released from the constraints of the court and eagerly sought to develop new markets. In 1928 eight of the leading artists formed a group called Yueman hui (Full Moon Society), as they met to exchange ideas during the full moon. This group later became known as Zhushan Bayou (Eight friends of Zhushan), comprised of Wang Qi, Cheng Yiting, Deng Bishan, Wang Dafan, Wang Yeting, He Xuren, Bi Botao, Xu Zhongnan and Tian Hexian.
Wang Qi (1884-1937), a native of Xinjianxian, Jiangxi province, went to Jingdezhen at the age of seventeen and was the founding member of Zhushan Bayou. The development of his mature style can be traced to a trip he made to Shanghai in 1916 to see an exhibition of paintings by the Yangzhou Baguai (Eight Eccentrics of Yangzhou). Wang was so impressed by the paintings of Huang Shen, one of the Eight Eccentrics, that he started to emulate Huangâs style in porcelain design. This influence can be seen in the present lot with his use of rapid and expressive brushstrokes to create whimsical, exaggerated figures with calligraphic inscriptions in cursive script, all within a sparse setting. By fusing Huangâs style with Western painting techniques, such as the use of light and shade, Wangâs personal style emerged. Comparable panels include a set of four sold in our New York rooms, 17th-18th March 2015, lot 295; and another included in the exhibition Brush and Clay. Chinese Porcelain of the Early 20th Century, Hong Kong Museum of Art, Hong Kong, 1990, cat. no. 29.
Deng Bishan (1874-1930), a native of Yuganxian, Jiangxi province, excelled in painting fish swimming amongst aquatic plants in a style that reflects a degree of Japanese influence. Well educated and a skilled calligrapher, he was highly respected by porcelain painters in Jingdezhen, teaching Wang Qi calligraphy and portrait painting on porcelain. A set of four fish plaques, from the collection of the Hon. Andrew Li Kwok Nang, was sold at Christieâs Hong Kong, 1st December 2010, lot 2832; and another was included in the exhibition ibid., cat. no. 82, together with four smaller plaques, cat. nos 78-81.

The term Simeiju derives from the seventh-century Preface to the Prince of Teng's Pavilion by Wang Bo. Apparently itself derived from the 'Four Beauties' of fifth-century poet Xie Lingyun, the phrase is taken to describe the features of the perfect gathering (an auspicious day, beautiful scenery, a joyful mood, and pleasant activities) and adopted a millenium later by the Qianlong Emperor (r. 1736-1795) to describe four of his favourite paintings, formerly in the collection of the late Ming collector Gu Congyi. These four works (Dream Journey on the Xiao-Xiang River; The Shu River; Nine Songs; and the Admonsitions of the Instructress) were enshrined in the Jingyixuan and impressed with Simeiju seals.
Compare a closely related imperial Simeiju seal mark from the Qianlong reign recorded in Guo Fuxiang, Ming Qing di hou xiyin [Imperial seals of the Ming and Qing dynasties], Beijing, 2003, vol. 5, p. 22; and a Jiaqing rendition, ibid., vol. 8, p. 38.
